idiom_name: Thread::SizedQueue(max) - push blocks while full, pop blocks while empty
implementation_notes: Ruby ships the pattern in core: Thread::SizedQueue.new(max) is a bounded blocking queue where push/enq/<</block until a slot frees and pop/deq/shift block until an item arrives (non_block: true raises ThreadError instead of waiting), while its unbounded sibling Thread::Queue differs only on the producer side. close is the built-in end-of-stream signal - threads blocked in push are interrupted with ClosedQueueError, and pop returns nil once the queue is drained - and max=/num_waiting expose resizing and waiter counts at runtime. Because SizedQueue is implemented in C (thread_sync.c), it is the ordinary choice; hand-writing a Mutex plus ConditionVariable buffer is only worth it for a non-FIFO policy. The GVL still serializes Ruby-level execution, so the queue decouples rates and overlaps I/O rather than parallelizing CPU work.
code_sketch:
jobs = Thread::SizedQueue.new(100)

Thread.new { items.each { |i| jobs.push(i) } }   # blocks while full
4.times.map do
  Thread.new { loop { handle(jobs.pop) } }      # blocks while empty
end.each(&:join)
# shutdown: jobs.close -> pushers raise ClosedQueueError, pops drain to nil
pitfalls: Thread::Queue (as opposed to SizedQueue) is unbounded: a fast producer grows the array until memory runs out.
An exception inside a consumer thread kills only that thread and stays silent until join; use Thread.abort_on_exception or a hand-off of results/errors.
After close, blocked pushers raise ClosedQueueError and pop returns nil once drained - code must distinguish 'closed and empty' from a legitimate nil item.
The GVL serializes Ruby execution, so threads plus a queue give I/O overlap and rate decoupling, not parallel CPU work (JRuby/TruffleRuby aside).
